item.title: Soil proteogenomics uncover microbial strategies for soil depth-specific carbon cycling under whole-soil warming conditions
item.dc:creator: Ulas Karaoz
Ricardo J. E. Alves
Nikola Tolic
Rosalie K. Chu
Carrie Nicora
Jason Toyoda
Emiley Eloe-Fadrosh
Margaret S. Torn
item.description:
Authors: Ulas Karaoz, Ricardo J. E. Alves, Nikola Tolic, Rosalie K. Chu, Carrie Nicora, Jason Toyoda, Emiley Eloe-Fadrosh, Margaret S. Torn, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10740
Abstract: Abstract Soils are Earth’s largest carbon reservoir, yet microbial mechanisms controlling decomposition, and their warming response, remain poorly resolved, especially in subsoils. Using genome-resolved proteogenomics within a replicated whole-soil warming experiment (0–90 cm, +4 °C, 7.5 years) we map microbial traits, their depth stratification, and warming responses. Depth is the dominant driver of microbial community and trait structure. Depth-wise, metabolism converge on low-molecular-weight and C1 compounds, challenging glucose-centric models, with surface soils enriched in methanol oxidation and deep soils in alcohol fermentation, CO oxidation and N₂ fixation. Abundant sialidases in deep soils implicate glycoproteins as a key carbon source. Warming effects are smaller and decrease over time but are depth-specific: surface soils show enhanced amino sugar and sugar alcohol transport, phosphorus mobilization, and stress tolerance, whereas mid- and deep soils exhibit stimulated C1 metabolism, CO oxidation, and altered nitrogen turnover. These depth-specific microbial trait shifts may critically influence soil carbon–climate feedbacks.

item.title: Anomalous spin–lattice coupling in a 2D antiferromagnetic semiconductor revealed by surface acoustic Rayleigh waves
item.dc:creator: Zahra Ebrahim Nataj
Md Sabbir Hossen Bijoy
Vladislav Korostelev
Jordan Teeter
Dylan Wright
Mohammad Zeinolabedini
Konstantin Klyukin
Fariborz Kargar
item.description:
Authors: Zahra Ebrahim Nataj, Md Sabbir Hossen Bijoy, Vladislav Korostelev, Jordan Teeter, Dylan Wright, Mohammad Zeinolabedini, Konstantin Klyukin, Fariborz Kargar, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Magnetic order in van der Waals magnets can strongly influence their lattice dynamics, yet how it affects local and macroscopic manifestations of spin-phonon coupling remains unclear. Optical phonons probe bond-scale exchange modulation and short-range spin correlations, whereas long-wavelength acoustic modes couple to uniform strain fields and are sensitive to renormalization of the macroscopic elastic tensor associated with long-range magnetic order. Experimentally accessing these acoustic excitations in low-dimensional crystals is challenging due to their low energies and the small lateral dimensions of exfoliated samples. Here, we employ Brillouin–Mandelstam scattering spectroscopy to investigate surface acoustic phonons in exfoliated NiPS 3 thin films across the antiferromagnetic transition. Our results show a single Rayleigh surface mode whose phase velocity decreases significantly across the Néel temperature. This anomaly reflects a strong magnetoelastic renormalization of the elastic constants triggered by the onset of antiferromagnetic order. First-principles calculations, combined with continuum finite-element modeling reproduce the Rayleigh-wave dispersion and its magnetic-order–induced shift. The results reveal how microscopic exchange interactions govern the macroscopic elastic response of two-dimensional antiferromagnetic semiconductors, enabling magnetically tunable phononic, magnonic, and strain-mediated spintronic devices.

item.title: Sleep forms flexible context representations in toddlers
item.dc:creator: Lisa Bastian
Eva-Maria Kurz
Lilli Gutjahr
Hannes Noack
Jan Born
item.description:
Authors: Lisa Bastian, Eva-Maria Kurz, Lilli Gutjahr, Hannes Noack, Jan Born
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10699
Abstract: Abstract Sleep consolidates episodic memory through a hippocampus-dependent process in adults. Whether and how sleep supports memory consolidation during early life, when hippocampal function is immature, remains unclear. Here, we examined effects of sleep on the consolidation of spatial context, a core component of episodic memory, in toddlers aged 2–3 years. Toddlers were familiarized with two spatial contexts, followed by a ~ 90-min nap or equivalent wake period. Afterwards, using a hide-and-seek game we tested their ability to relocate toys within these contexts. Only after post-familiarization sleep, toddlers showed significant context memory and formed stronger associations between toys and specific contexts compared to wakefulness. Contextual memory was positively correlated with spindle density and slow oscillation–spindle phase-amplitude coupling during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Here, we show that, despite hippocampal immaturity, memory effects in the sleeping toddler’s brain are accompanied by thalamo-cortical oscillatory dynamics that are also implicated in adult memory consolidation.

item.title: Interpretable AI-guided discovery of degradable ionizable lipids with enhanced hepatic mRNA delivery in vivo
item.dc:creator: Zhen Zhang
Yongbo Ren
Deqiang Kong
Jindong Feng

item.description:
Authors: Zhen Zhang, Yongbo Ren, Deqiang Kong, Jindong Feng, Kaiyi Hu, Xinyun Xu, Fukang Deng, Peixia Li, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable RNA medicines, yet ionizable-lipid discovery remains largely empirical, particularly when in vitro activity must be translated into functional hepatic delivery in vivo. Here we establish an interpretable discovery framework that combines modular degradable lipid chemistry, high-throughput phenotyping, machine learning, virtual library expansion, and independent in vivo validation to define a learnable ionizable-lipid design space. Starting from a 520-member library, we train an XGBoost model on firefly luciferase (Fluc) expression in HeLa cells and use physicochemical descriptors and molecular fingerprints to prospectively prioritize candidates with higher predicted in vitro transfection activity across a 10,920-member virtual space. In vivo phenotyping subsequently identifies PA97MD101 as a lead ionizable lipid. In mice, PA97MD101 enhances hepatic mRNA expression and Cre-dependent recombination and supports Cas9/sgTtr-mediated TTR suppression. Its performance is associated with pH-dependent membrane activity and reduced lysosomal colocalization. These findings support further evaluation of PA97MD101 for functional hepatic RNA delivery.

item.title: Ultrahigh-speed chromatically band-limited illumination profilometry
item.dc:creator: Cheng Jiang
Jinyang Liang
item.description:
Authors: Cheng Jiang, Jinyang Liang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Single-shot fringe projection profilometry (SS-FPP) has been extensively applied to the study of rapid three-dimensional (3D) dynamics in physics, engineering, and biology. Despite these advancements, the imaging capability of time-resolved SS-FPP is still limited by the flexibility and speed of both pattern projection and image acquisition, as well as by the duration of the observation time window. Here, we overcome these constraints by developing chromatically band-limited illumination profilometry (C-BLIP). On the illumination side, C-BLIP projects programmable grayscale fringes at ultrahigh speed by synergizing a digital micromirror device with a user-selectable encoding region of interest and a custom-designed projection lens for chromatically band-limited illumination with incoherent light sources. On the detection side, C-BLIP acquires spatially multiplexed color fringe images, followed by 3D image reconstruction. Using C-BLIP, we demonstrated color 3D imaging of a turbofan blade-projectile collision at 25 thousand frames per second (kfps), as well as intensity 3D imaging of maple samara’s fall aerodynamics at 75 kfps and ultrasound encryption/recovery at 150 kfps. These results highlight C-BLIP’s promise for continuous-streaming, ultrahigh-speed 3D metrology in industrial inspection, bionics, and data security.

item.title: C-terminal evolutionary remodelling of isoleucyl-tRNA synthetases is a prokaryote-specific strategy for tuning aminoacylation rate
item.dc:creator: Petra Modrusan
Alojzije Brkic
Andre Lecona Buttelli
Marc Leibundgut
Igor Zivkovic
Nenad Ban
Liam M. Longo
Ita Gruic-Sovulj
item.description:
Authors: Petra Modrusan, Alojzije Brkic, Andre Lecona Buttelli, Marc Leibundgut, Igor Zivkovic, Nenad Ban, Liam M. Longo, Ita Gruic-Sovulj
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are the guardians of translational fidelity. Their complex function is mirrored by an elaborate structure, which includes multiple nested domains. While the evolutionary pressures that promoted the emergence of some domains, such as the editing domain, are clear, the pressures acting on other domains, particularly those at the C-terminus, are not. Here, we combine kinetic analysis, X-ray crystallography, and bioinformatics to unveil the history and evolutionary forces that have shaped isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS) domain structure. We find that the traditional classification of IleRSs based on the C-terminal tRNA-recognition domains is incomplete, as it fails to capture features of the synthetic domain. Guided by a crystal structure of the Priestia megaterium IleRS2:tRNA Ile complex, we removed key interactions between IleRS2 and its cognate tRNA and characterised their impact on enzyme activity. We found that D-loop interactions with the IleRS2 C-terminal domains are non-essential in prokaryotes, and their loss can even increase catalytic turnover. Further, we show that the zinc-binding domain of IleRS1 recognises the anticodon less stringently than the canonical C-terminal domain of IleRS2. Our data suggest that C-terminal evolutionary remodelling of IleRSs is an ongoing process with a historical precedent and is consistent with selection for faster aminoacylation rate.

item.dc:creator: Stefan H. Mueller

item.description:
Authors: Stefan H. Mueller, David M. Grimson, Holden Paz, Aidan C. Fitch, Haibo Yu, Marco Ribezzi-Crivellari, Andrew D. Griffiths, Antoine M. van Oijen, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Single-molecule techniques provide exceptional resolution of biomolecular dynamics but are limited by low throughput. Here, we present a DNA barcoding strategy that enables parallel kinetic profiling of multiple protein variants in a single experiment. Each protein is covalently linked to a unique DNA barcode, decoded through transient hybridisation of fluorescent probes distinguished by colour and binding duration. Applied to a library of 16 ClpS variants, this approach revealed ~5-fold variation in dissociation kinetics and uncovered previously unrecognised bimodal binding behaviour arising from distinct structural subpopulations. By enabling scalable, multiplexed functional characterisation at the single-molecule level, this platform provides a general framework for protein engineering, directed evolution and the development of next-generation single-molecule technologies.

item.title: Ki-67, the chromosome periphery and de-compartmentalisation each contribute to nucleophosmin mislocalisation in acute myeloid leukaemia
item.dc:creator: Martin Grundy
Peter Woodmancy
Kellie Lucken
Xiaomeng Xing
Robert Markus
Seema Bagia
Sarah Storr
Claire H. Seedhouse
item.description:
Authors: Martin Grundy, Peter Woodmancy, Kellie Lucken, Xiaomeng Xing, Robert Markus, Seema Bagia, Sarah Storr, Claire H. Seedhouse, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The mitotic chromosome periphery (MCP) is an important chromosome compartment but links to disease remains elusive. Here we define the mitosis-specific, Ki-67 interactome, identifying additional MCP components and revealing that MCP genes are commonly mutated in cancer, including nucleophosmin (NPM1). Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)-specific NPM1 mutations (NPM1c + ), result in protein mislocalisation (nucleolus to cytoplasm). We demonstrate that NPM1c+ fails to adequately bind to the MCP, instead forming aggregates during mitosis. We also report that, de-compartmentalisation at mitotic onset allows formation of NPM1wt/c+ multimers. These mislocalisation mechanisms contribute to a significant hinderance of NPM1 re-entry into daughter cell nucleoli. Enhancing MCP loading capacity via Ki-67 overexpression resulted in increased MCP-bound NPM1c+ during mitosis and greater yield of nucleolar NPM1c + . Ki-67 expression demonstrated a significant interaction with NPM1 mutation status on AML patient overall survival, whereby higher Ki-67 was associated with increased hazard in NPM1wt but reduced hazard in NPM1c+ patients. This work reveals mechanistic insight into AML and evidence that the MCP has untapped therapeutic potential.

item.title: Block-fitness modeling of the global air mobility network
item.dc:creator: Giulia Fischetti
Anna Mancini
Giulio Cimini
Jessica T. Davis
Abby O. K. Leung
Alessandro Vespignani
Guido Caldarelli
item.description:
Authors: Giulia Fischetti, Anna Mancini, Giulio Cimini, Jessica T. Davis, Abby O. K. Leung, Alessandro Vespignani, Guido Caldarelli
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Accurate representations of origin-destination (OD) passenger flows on the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, OD data are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model that treats air mobility as a stochastic process within a sparse maximum-entropy framework, informed by aggregate traffic volumes of individual locations and geographic regions. The model accurately reconstructs both network structure and mobility flows, yielding epidemic spreading trajectories that closely match those obtained using real mobility data. Furthermore, the method can be effectively implemented using open data on flight routes and airport traffic, reducing dependence on proprietary datasets. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for scenario analysis and policy design in global mobility systems.

item.title: Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model
item.dc:creator: Mattia Poinelli
Eric Rignot
Hélène Seroussi
Joshua Cuzzone
Tyler Pelle
Eric Larour
item.description:
Authors: Mattia Poinelli, Eric Rignot, Hélène Seroussi, Joshua Cuzzone, Tyler Pelle, Eric Larour
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10364
Abstract: Abstract Thwaites Glacier is a major contributor to Antarctic mass loss and a key source of uncertainty in future sea-level rise. Ocean-driven melting at its grounding line drives rapid retreat, yet most models treat the transition between grounded and floating ice as a sharp boundary, neglecting kilometer-scale seawater intrusions that develop as the grounding line migrates and forms a grounding zone. Here, we show that actively-melting grounding zones are required to reproduce nearly three decades of observed retreat, thinning, and acceleration of Thwaites Glacier in a calibrated ice-sheet model, with successful reconstruction occurring only when grounding zones are represented as 2-5 km wide regions. Extending this model forward, we show that grounding-zone processes govern glacier’s detachment from stabilizing seafloor ridges, enabling unpinning as early as 2038 and producing up to 30 ± 6 mm of global mean sea-level rise by 2100 - approximately double previous projections even without additional climate warming.

item.title: Precision functional mapping of imagined and experienced pain
item.dc:creator: Michael Sun
Bogdan Petre
Ke Bo
Carmen I. Bango
Malka Hershkop
Sydney L. Shohan
Heejung Jung
Tor D. Wager
item.description:
Authors: Michael Sun, Bogdan Petre, Ke Bo, Carmen I. Bango, Malka Hershkop, Sydney L. Shohan, Heejung Jung, Tor D. Wager
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Imagination is a principal human capacity, enabling simulation of sensations and situations for planning, learning, and empathy. We examined neural representations of experienced and imagined pain across eight body sites using deep-phenotyping, precision functional MRI with over seven hours of scanning per participant (N = 9). Here we show, using conventional mapping, pattern classification, and representational similarity analyses, that both imagined and experienced pain activated nociceptive regions (e.g., dorsoposterior insula) and non-nociceptive regions (e.g., premotor areas and inferior inter-effector motor cortex). However, imagined pain did not reliably reactivate body site-selective nociceptive patterns in any region. Instead, imagined and experienced pain shared multivariate representations across widespread cortical and subcortical regions, particularly transmodal cortical areas including dorsomedial and lateral prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus. These findings suggest that imagination generates distributed pain-like activity, but with separable neural codes for imagined and experienced pain. This distinction may explain the difficulty of vividly imagining pain and clarify its potential roles in empathy, planning, and pain chronification.

item.title: Structures and molecular mechanisms of RAD54B in modulating homologous recombination
item.dc:creator: Pengtao Liang
Stephanie Tye
Johanna Ertl da Costa
Neelam Maharshi
Bilge Argunhan
Lucas Kuhlen
Megan Battley
Elizabeth A. McCormack
item.description:
Authors: Pengtao Liang, Stephanie Tye, Johanna Ertl da Costa, Neelam Maharshi, Bilge Argunhan, Lucas Kuhlen, Megan Battley, Elizabeth A. McCormack, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Genome stability is essential for cellular viability yet constantly threatened by DNA-damaging agents. Among these, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are particularly harmful and in S/G2 phases are faithfully repaired through homologous recombination (HR). The RAD51 recombinase forms nucleoprotein filaments on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) that performs critical functions in HR. The efficiency of HR depends on precise regulation of RAD51 filament dynamics by accessory factors, including RAD54B, a double-strand DNA-dependent ATPase. Here, using cryogenic electron microscopy, mutagenesis, and biochemical assays, we show that RAD54B stabilizes RAD51–DNA filaments, inhibits RAD51 ATPase activity, and promotes D-loop formation and strand exchange. RAD54B contains two main RAD51-interacting sites and a β-domain that bridges RAD51 protomers, is positioned to contact donor dsDNA, and regulates RAD54B’s ATPase activity. Cellular assays reveal that the RAD51-interacting sites are required for repairing DSBs by HR in human cells. Our findings uncover a modular architecture and mechanistic framework for RAD54B’s critical role in genome maintenance.

item.title: Short Wavelength Infrared Diimmonium Nano-Agents for Photoacoustic Imaging
item.dc:creator: Longcai Liu
Yang Chen
Liya Yu
Xiaozhou Mou
Guangxue Feng
Yu Cai
item.description:
Authors: Longcai Liu, Yang Chen, Liya Yu, Xiaozhou Mou, Guangxue Feng, Yu Cai
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Photoacoustic imaging (PAI) as an innovative biomedical imaging modality shows high contrast and superior spatial resolution, yet remains limited by underdeveloped second near-infrared (NIR-II, 1000-1700 nm) contrast agents, particularly neglecting the NIR-IIb (1500-1700 nm) window. In this work, we designed a new class of diimmonium (DB)-based dicationic nano-agents (DB·2X, X = TFSI - , B(C 2 O 4 ) 2 - , or BF 4 - ) for 1700 nm excitation PAI. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that dicationic DB 2+ exhibits a dramatically reduced excitation energy (1.24 eV) and enhanced oscillator strength (f = 1.11) by molecular engineering, attributed to a symmetry-allowed local excitation mechanism for electronic restructuring. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction further demonstrates the intermolecular spacings >5.0 Å in DB·2X aggregates, facilitating optimized non-radiative transitions for amplified PAI signals. In vivo study using different disease models shows that DB·2TFSI nano-agents under 1700 nm excitation can achieve higher signal-to-background ratio and minimized interference from endogenous chromophores compared to conventional 1064 nm excitation. Biocompatibility assessments confirm low cytotoxicity, underscoring potential for further development of DB·2TFSI nano-agents. This work delivers a robust molecular design paradigm for non-radiative decay optimization, and for the first time establishes 1700 nm-excitable PAI nano-agents, paving the way for tissue high-quality biomedical imaging.

item.title: Discrete subdomains establish epigenetic diversity in subtelomeric heterochromatin in fission yeast
item.dc:creator: Agnisrota Mazumder
John Cooper
Can Goksal
Rosario Y. J. Brockhausen
Jonas M. Schauß
Jasbeer S. Khanduja
Richard I. Joh
Ahmed A. A. Amine
item.description:
Authors: Agnisrota Mazumder, John Cooper, Can Goksal, Rosario Y. J. Brockhausen, Jonas M. Schauß, Jasbeer S. Khanduja, Richard I. Joh, Ahmed A. A. Amine, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Subtelomeres are imperfect repeats adjacent to telomeres that are transcriptionally repressed by heterochromatin. Although essential for genome integrity, their repetitive nature has thwarted dissection of local heterochromatin assembly and maintenance mechanisms. By engineering fission yeast strains carrying fluorescent reporters at a single subtelomere, we uncovered distinct subdomains. These subdomains have different silencing requirements: telomere-proximal regions rely on canonical shelterin- or RNAi-dependent nucleation pathways, whereas telomere-distal regions involve nucleosome remodelers, histone chaperones, and boundary-associated factors. Subdomains also exhibit discrete epigenetic states emerging both at homologous loci on different chromosome arms and along the same subtelomeric sequence. We document these epigenetic states using multi-generational live imaging and targeted perturbations. These analyses show that subtelomeric subdomains display position-specific, clonally variable silencing across a spectrum from robust to fragile epigenetic states. Interestingly, structural variants, common in subtelomeric sequences across eukaryotes, dictate local epigenetic stability. These findings reveal that subtelomeres, long recognized for their sequence variability, form a dynamic mosaic of coexisting epigenetic domains. This implies a wide range of gene-repressive regulatory logic at the chromosome ends, from environmental responsiveness to silencing stability.

item.title: The central coupler of ClpXP controls intersubunit communication and couples intrasubunit chemical energy with force generation
item.dc:creator: Robert P. Sosa
Alfredo Jose Florez Ariza
Jeonghoon Kim
Alexander B. Tong
Zhen-Hui Kang
Alicia Li
John Kuriyan
Carlos Bustamante
item.description:
Authors: Robert P. Sosa, Alfredo Jose Florez Ariza, Jeonghoon Kim, Alexander B. Tong, Zhen-Hui Kang, Alicia Li, John Kuriyan, Carlos Bustamante
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract ClpX is a clockwise hexameric helical arrangement that hydrolyzes ATP to unfold proteins and translocate them into the proteolytic chamber. We investigate the central coupler, a three α-helix module conserved among AAA+ ATPases, which is proposed to enable intersubunit communication and mechanochemical coupling. Although fundamental in AAA+ ATPases, the molecular mechanism underlying these processes remains elusive in ClpX. By combining single-molecule optical tweezers, biochemical assays and single-particle cryo-EM we demonstrate that the central coupler, of the second-highest subunit of the ClpX clockwise helical arrangement, positions its Arginine-finger, sensor-I and sensor-II to contact the ATP of the anticlockwise neighbor subunit to trigger its hydrolysis. Then, the central coupler of the highest subunit rapidly couples the ATP hydrolysis with the downward motion of its substrate-translocating loop, enabling fast force generation to swiftly unfold protein substrates while maximizing the thermodynamic efficiency of the motor.

Abstract: Abstract Understanding how wild populations undergo rapid phenotypic evolution requires linking phenotypic change to its underlying genomic architecture over contemporary timescales. Authors: Gabriele Bressanini, Yue Ma, Michael Hanks, Hyukjoon Kwon, M. S. Kim
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Analogue quantum simulators offer a promising route to explore quantum many-body dynamics beyond classical reach in the near term. However, their vulnerability to noise limits the accuracy of simulations. Here, we establish a continuous-time framework for mitigating noise in analogue quantum simulation. Furthermore, the protocol is Hamiltonian-independent and robust to realistic ancilla noise. This work points to a promising direction for achieving high-fidelity analogue quantum simulation in the presence of noise.

Abstract: Abstract Fungal necromass, particularly dead microbial cells rich in melanin, is an important contributor to long-term soil carbon stabilization. Abstract: Abstract Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Abstract: Abstract Many nanosized metals with limited dislocation nucleation and multiplication usually exhibit poor plasticity. Previous studies have demonstrated that multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) can achieve a combination of strength and plasticity. Abstract: Abstract Hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a key public health challenge, particularly among people who use and inject drugs (PWUD, PWID). Incidence among PWID decreased from 6.5 (4.1–8.0) to 2.4 (1.4–4.2) per 100 person-years. These reductions likely reflect the combined impact of DAA scale-up and harm reduction policies, marking substantial progress toward elimination targets. However, ongoing transmission highlights persistent barriers requiring targeted public health actions.

Abstract: Abstract Adaptive radiations provide powerful models to study the origins of phenotypic novelty and species diversity. Abstract: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Abstract: Abstract The diversification of herbivorous dinosaurs and the rise of angiosperms in the Late Cretaceous are each well established, but the link between them is debated. Broad-scale diversity patterns in the two groups appear not to closely align, and there is no direct evidence of dinosaur adaptation to angiosperm-based diets. These modifications enabled extensive oral processing of soft food using anteroposterior movement of the mandible and occlusion of ridges and grooves on opposed elements. Altogether, this attests to a highly specialised herbivorous diet in caenagnathids, which likely consisted in large part of fleshy angiosperm fruits, which increased in size and diversity in concert with the radiation of oviraptorosaurs. Caenagnathids thus provide one of the strongest candidates for angiosperm-based diet adaptations in dinosaurs, but their role in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit—which shaped early Cenozoic flora—remains unclear.

Abstract: Abstract Multimodal fluorescence and phase imaging provides complementary information about biological samples. However, existing simultaneous fluorescence-phase techniques primarily operate in transmission mode and are limited to thin specimens, restricting their use in thick tissues and in vivo applications. Compared with state-of-the-art implicit neural fields, this approach improves computational speed, reconstruction accuracy, and interpretability. By pairing nanoscale resolution and local history with population-level statistics, the pipeline enables unbiased identification and quantification of degradation pathways across statistically meaningful particle sets. These findings show that maximal rectification is not always beneficial for quantum information, establishing a new principle for designing the fundamental properties of twisted superconductors towards low-power, high-fidelity quantum circuits.

Authors: Bangguo He, Ting Bai, Liyang Wang, Shuai Zhang, Wei Ying
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Efficient ammonium uptake is essential for plant growth and nitrogen-use efficiency, yet the structural basis of ammonium transport and regulation in plant AMTs remains unclear. Here, we determined multiple cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Arabidopsis thaliana ammonium transporter AMT1;1 in apo, ammonium-bound, methylammonium-bound, low-pH and phosphomimetic states. These structures reveal a conserved ammonium conduction pathway comprising an aromatic recruitment vestibule, a Phe-gate/Twin-His-containing pore, and a polar intracellular exit region. We further identified a conserved extracellular N-terminal disulfide bond required for oligomer stability and transport activity, suggesting potential redox-dependent regulation. On the cytoplasmic side, phosphorylation modulates C-terminal interactions with intracellular loops, revealing an allosteric regulatory mechanism. Comparison with the bacterial ammonium-sensing protein Sd -Amt1 uncovers a conserved ammonium-recognition region in At AMT1;1 that contributes to transport activity but lacks the signaling module and ligand-dependent conformational switching observed in Sd -Amt1. Together, these findings provide structural insight into ammonium transport and coordinated regulation in plant AMT transporters.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Histone 3 lysine 27-to-methionine substitutions (H3K27M) drive aggressive diffuse midline gliomas by blocking differentiation of radial glial progenitor cells committed to oligodendrogenesis. We establish prolonged differentiation as a powerful tool to uncover regulators of glioma cell states and demonstrate that the pioneer transcription factor (TF) ASCL1 is a key mediator of H3K27M-driven plasticity and tumorigenesis. Mechanistically, ASCL1 synergizes with H3K27M to redistribute the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to regulatory elements co-enriched for ASCL1 and SOX motifs, promoting expression of stem and neural progenitor genes at the expense of mesenchymal genes in DMGs. ASCL1 loss acts as a “fire exit”, enabling alternative differentiation despite H3K27M, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting stalled differentiation and tumor plasticity in histone-mutant gliomas and cancers with a stem cell hierarchy.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10655
Abstract: Abstract Desulfovibrio spp. are associated with inflammatory diseases and human health, yet limited representative genomes and isolates hinder our understanding of their role in disease. Here, we assembled a comprehensive database of 2658 Desulfovibrio genomes across 90 diseases and 32 countries, including 24 human isolates. Genomic analyses showed extensive species diversity and revealed disease-associated functional traits, including flagellin and adaptation-associated genes (i.e., ureases). Flagellin-mediated Toll-like receptor 5 activation was species-specific and D. desulfuricans flagellin downregulated TGF-beta signalling in murine small intestinal organoids, suggesting impaired immune tolerance. Additionally, we investigated genomic capacity for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) production, a main Desulfovibrio metabolite. While health- and disease-associated Desulfovibrio spp. mainly encoded dissimilatory sulfate reduction, tetrathionate metabolism-encoding bacteria were exclusively detected in inflammatory bowel diseases, including Proteus mirabilis and Morganella morganii . Overall, our study provides a comprehensive genomic Desulfovibrio resource and identifies new links associating strain variation, functional traits and H 2 S-production with inflammatory diseases.

Authors: Alice Y. Nam, Jiwook Shin, Morgan Tenney, Baihe Zhang, Y. Kate Hong
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Sensory inputs reach cortical and subcortical areas in parallel, but how they coordinate to guide decisions remains unknown. We examined the roles of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the superior colliculus (SC) in mice performing whisker-mediated tactile detection. While inactivating S1 contralateral to the stimulus increased detection threshold, inactivating ipsilateral S1 decreased it. These opposing effects reflected shifts in choice bias rather than sensitivity. Unilateral SC inactivation produced similar directional effects, whereas bilateral inactivation of either S1 or SC neutralized bias. Furthermore, SC lesions impaired detection performance, and combined S1 inactivation caused no further impairment, indicating that S1-mediated shifts in bias were SC-dependent. S1 inactivation also decreased sensory-evoked neural activity in SC, and choice decoding revealed that behavioral impairment was more closely associated with changes in SC population activity than with loss of sensory encoding in S1. Thus, S1 shapes perceptual bias by modulating SC-dependent circuits that transform sensory evidence into perceptual decisions.

Authors: Jiangong Zhu, Chao Yu, Yi Jiang, Wolfgang Schade, Martin Angelmahr, Xuezhe Wei, Haifeng Dai
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10700
Abstract: Abstract The safety assessment of battery systems is constrained by sparse temperature measurements and monolithic diagnostic frameworks in conventional battery management systems (BMS). To address this, we propose a multi-model collaborative thermal-runaway early-warning framework using distributed temperature sensing. An integrated sensing scheme increases temperature sensing points within the battery pack from 32 to 540 with minimal wiring complexity and is validated in real-world vehicle operation. We establish a functional relationship between temperature Shannon entropy (SE) and average temperature variation to derive a dynamic warning boundary incorporating error tolerance. Integrating this boundary with thresholds for temperature, temperature change rate, and SE change rate enables collaborative early warning. Compared with conventional BMS warning benchmarks, the framework provides maximum warning lead times of 706 s in laboratory modules and 554 s in real-world vehicle operation. These findings demonstrate the potential of distributed sensing and collaborative diagnostics for proactive thermal-runaway risk identification.

item.description:
Authors: Jiao Lin, Anthony Mu, Wei Tang, Feng Li, Yuwei Zhu, Mingqian Li, Ram Hemanth Yeerella, Christopher Potts, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Today’s lithium‑ion battery manufacturing heavily relies on polyvinylidene fluoride binder and N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone solvent-based processing, which incurs high cost and hinders environmental sustainability. While bio-derived binders enable aqueous processing, their reliance on hydrogen bonding alone limits mechanical strength and electrochemical stability. Here, we introduce a fluorine‑free, water‑processable binder comprised of polyacrylic acid and carboxymethyl cellulose crosslinked by citric acid. The network integrates hydrogen, covalent, and ionic bonding among binder chains, active particles, and current collectors, providing strong adhesion as well as good oxidative stability and thermal stability. LiFePO 4 positive electrodes fabricated with fluorine‑free binder deliver comparable initial capacity to the control electrodes with polyvinylidene fluoride binder, while providing better cycle stability. This chemistry applies to a wide range of positive and negative electrode materials. Importantly, the fluorine‑free binder further facilitates sustainable direct recycling, demonstrating full recovery of spent positive and negative electrodes to achieve the same level of performance with pristine materials without generating fluorinated residue. Life-cycle analysis shows significant reductions in energy cost and emissions compared with recycling polyvinylidene fluoride-based batteries. This binder strategy endows high performance with circularity, offering a scalable route to sustainable battery manufacturing technologies.

Authors: Thea F. Rogers, Jessica Stock, Natalie Grace Schulz, Gözde Yalçin, Simone Rencken, Anton Weissenbacher, Tereza Clarence, Darrin T. Schultz, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10319
Abstract: Abstract How genomic changes translate into organismal novelties is often confounded by the multi-layered nature of genome architecture and the long evolutionary timescales over which molecular changes can accumulate. Coleoid cephalopods (squid, cuttlefish, and octopus) provide a unique system to study these processes due to a large-scale chromosomal rearrangement in the coleoid ancestor that gave rise to highly modified karyotypes, followed by lineage-specific repeat expansions, fusions, and translocations. How these events have shaped gene regulatory patterns underlying the evolution of coleoid innovations, including their large and elaborately structured nervous systems, novel organs, and complex behaviours, remains poorly understood. To address this, we integrate Micro-C, RNA-seq, and ATAC-seq across multiple coleoid species, developmental stages, and tissues. We find that while chromatin domains are broadly conserved, hundreds of chromatin loops are species- and context-specific, with distinct regulation signatures and dynamic expression profiles. CRISPR–Cas9 knockout of a putative regulatory sequence within a conserved region demonstrates the role of loops in neural development and the prevalence of long-range interactions that extend beyond chromatin domains. We propose that differential evolutionary constraints across the coleoid 3D genome allow macroevolutionary processes to shape genome topology in distinct ways, facilitating the emergence of novel regulatory entanglements and ultimately contributing to the evolution and maintenance of complex traits in the coleoids.

Authors: Gabriel Mendoza-Rojas, Philip Nakonz, Min Lu, Nora Marie Kühne, Johannes Postma, Naomi Shtakser, Max Heinen, Manav Patel, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10652
Abstract: Abstract A successful infection requires pathogens to recognize the specific host environment in order to reprogram their physiology accordingly. One major way in which eukaryotic cells sense their surroundings is via G-Protein Coupled Receptors (GPCRs), which share a seven-transmembrane architecture and G-protein-mediated downstream signaling. While mammalian GPCRs are well-characterized and represent important drug targets, their fungal counterparts remain poorly understood. Here we uncover a GPCR-based mechanism that allows the corn pathogen Ustilago maydis to sense whether it has entered plant tissue. During infection, the fungus secretes the protein Pit2, which is cleaved by host apoplastic cysteine proteases, releasing a peptide ligand ‘hidden’ within the protein core. This ligand activates the fungal GPCR Gpe1, thus promoting fungal proliferation after initial host penetration. We elucidate the crystal structure of Pit2 and model the complex formed by Gpe1 and the Pit2-derived peptide. Structure-guided mutational analysis supports that disrupting this interaction reduces fungal virulence. The Gpe1/Pit2 system is conserved in related fungal species, with co-evolutionary signatures apparently preserving receptor-ligand specificity. Furthermore, this system shows mechanistic similarities to mammalian receptors, suggesting an evolutionary link between fungal and mammalian GPCRs.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Cas9 is a metal-dependent nuclease used for genome editing across diverse cells and organisms exhibiting distinct ionic environments, yet how metal ions regulate its catalytic function, and consequently its editing efficiency remains unclear. Mutations targeting the DBP disrupt HNH activation and impair the coupled catalytic activity of both nucleases, identifying the pocket as a key regulator of Cas9’s metal-dependent activity. Together with quantum–classical simulations revealing distinct catalytic behaviours among divalent metals, these findings uncover an ion-dependent regulatory mechanism in Cas9 with insights for genome editing across diverse biological environments.
